title: Given a monolithic (e.g. food-delivery) application, how would you decompose it into microservices (DDD bounded contexts, database-per-service, extract one module at a time), and what challenges do you face?

s1_definition.profdef: Decomposing a monolith means carving a single large application into independently deployable services along meaningful business boundaries rather than technical layers. The disciplined approach uses Domain-Driven Design to find bounded contexts, assigns each context its own service with a private database, and extracts one module at a time using the Strangler Fig pattern so the monolith keeps running throughout. The main challenges are splitting a shared database without breaking foreign-key integrity, replacing in-process calls and local transactions with network calls and sagas, keeping data consistent through events, and avoiding premature or overly fine-grained splits that create a distributed monolith.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture National Bank of India as one huge building where accounts, payments, loans, and notifications all share the same giant ledger room. Decomposing it is like moving each department into its own building with its own ledger, one department at a time, while the bank stays open the whole time. You start by drawing clear department boundaries (bounded contexts), you give each department its own books (database-per-service), and you move the easiest, least-connected department first. The hard parts are untangling the shared ledger, teaching departments to send couriers instead of walking across the room (network calls and sagas), and not splitting so finely that every tiny task needs five couriers.
s1_definition.oneliner: Decompose along DDD bounded contexts, give each service a private database, extract one module at a time with the Strangler Fig, and expect the hard parts to be the shared database and the shift from local transactions to sagas.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Decomposing a monolith means carving a single large application into independently deployable services along meaningful business boundaries rather than technical layers. The disciplined approach uses Domain-Driven Design to find bounded contexts, assigns each context its own service with a private database, and extracts one module at a time using the Strangler Fig pattern so the monolith keeps running throughout. The main challenges are splitting a shared database without breaking foreign-key integrity, replacing in-process calls and local transactions with network calls and sagas, keeping data consistent through events, and avoiding premature or overly fine-grained splits that create a distributed monolith.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture National Bank of India as one huge building where accounts, payments, loans, and notifications all share the same giant ledger room. Decomposing it is like moving each department into its own building with its own ledger, one department at a time, while the bank stays open the whole time. You start by drawing clear department boundaries (bounded contexts), you give each department its own books (database-per-service), and you move the easiest, least-connected department first. The hard parts are untangling the shared ledger, teaching departments to send couriers instead of walking across the room (network calls and sagas), and not splitting so finely that every tiny task needs five couriers.

**One line to remember:** Decompose along DDD bounded contexts, give each service a private database, extract one module at a time with the Strangler Fig, and expect the hard parts to be the shared database and the shift from local transactions to sagas.

sections.s2_technical:
Start by finding boundaries, not by cutting code. Use Domain-Driven Design to identify bounded contexts, which are areas of the business with their own language and rules, for example Account, Payment, Loan, and Notification in a bank. Each bounded context becomes a candidate service. You decompose by business capability, so the boundary is "payments" not "the controllers layer", because splitting by technical layer gives you a distributed monolith where every feature still spans every service.

Pick the extraction order deliberately. Extract the module with the fewest dependencies first, or the one that most needs independent scaling, so you get an early win and learn the mechanics on something low-risk. Use the Strangler Fig pattern: put a facade or gateway in front, route the extracted capability to the new service, and leave everything else hitting the monolith. Over time you strangle the monolith capability by capability until it is gone. The monolith never has a big-bang rewrite.

Splitting the database is the hardest part. In the monolith, tables are joined freely and foreign keys enforce integrity. When Payment moves out, it can no longer join the accounts table. You give Payment its own database and replace the join with either a synchronous call to the Account Service or a local read model kept fresh by consuming `account-events` from Kafka. Shared reference data is duplicated, and integrity that used to be a foreign key becomes an application-level check plus eventual reconciliation.

Then handle transactions and consistency. A monolith transfer is one `@Transactional` method; once Payment and Account are separate you cannot span a transaction across them, so you use the Saga pattern with compensating actions and accept eventual consistency. Finally, expect operational and testing challenges: more pipelines, service discovery, distributed tracing with a shared traceId, and contract tests so a change in one service does not silently break another. The senior-level nuance is restraint: decompose only where teams genuinely need independent deployment or scaling, extract incrementally, and be willing to stop or merge back if a boundary creates coordination without autonomy.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs one monolith handling accounts, payments, and notifications against a single shared database. Problem 1 — the payments module needs to scale for festival-season load, but because everything is one deployable, scaling payments means scaling accounts and notifications too, wasting resources. This is exactly why we extract Payment as its own service that scales independently. Problem 2 — the payments code freely joins the accounts table, so it cannot simply move out. This is exactly the shared-database challenge, solved by giving Payment its own store and calling the Account Service. Problem 3 — a transfer was one local transaction; after the split it spans two services. This is exactly why we introduce a saga.

The mini-project simulates the extraction. It models the `MonolithApp` with everything inside, then a `StranglerFacade` that routes payment calls to a newly extracted `PaymentService` while account and notification calls still go to the monolith, with `PaymentService` owning its own data and calling an `AccountServiceClient`. A runnable demo shows a payment served by the new service, an account lookup still served by the monolith, and the saga compensating a failed step.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a payment of 50,000 rupees from Rajesh (SAV2001), an account lookup for the same account, and then the same payment while the Account Service is down.

Step 1: The payment request arrives at the Strangler Facade with path `/payments`. The facade routes it to the newly extracted Payment Service, not the monolith. This is the Strangler Fig in action: one capability has moved out.

Step 2: The Payment Service runs its saga. It calls the Account Service to debit Rajesh, which is a remote call that replaces the old in-database join. On success it records the payment in its own private database and returns COMPLETED.

Step 3: An account lookup arrives with path `/accounts`. The facade routes it to the monolith, which still owns accounts and notifications. This shows the monolith and the new service running side by side during migration.

Step 4: The Account Service is now simulated as down. The payment request routes to the Payment Service again, but the remote debit throws because the dependency is unavailable.

Step 5: The saga catches the failure, writes no local payment record, and returns FAILED. Because there was no successful debit, there is nothing to compensate, and consistency is preserved without any single cross-service transaction.

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Request arrives
    │
    ▼
  StranglerFacade (routing decision)
    │
    ├─ path /payments ──→ EXTRACTED Payment Service (new, own DB)
    │                         │ saga: debit via AccountServiceClient
    │                         ├─ success → record payment → COMPLETED
    │                         └─ debit fails → nothing recorded → FAILED
    │
    └─ path /accounts ──→ LEGACY Monolith (still owns accounts + notif)

                              ▼
  Over time: more paths move left (strangled) until monolith is empty
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I decompose a monolith, I start by finding boundaries, not by cutting code. I use Domain-Driven Design to identify bounded contexts, which are areas of the business with their own language and rules, such as Account, Payment, Loan, and Notification at National Bank of India. Each bounded context becomes a candidate service, and I decompose by business capability rather than by technical layer, because splitting by layer just produces a distributed monolith where every feature still spans every service.

I never do a big-bang rewrite. I use the Strangler Fig pattern: I put a gateway or facade in front, route one extracted capability to a new service, and leave everything else hitting the monolith. I extract one module at a time, usually starting with the one that has the fewest dependencies or the one that most needs independent scaling, so I get an early win and learn the mechanics on something low-risk. Over time I strangle the monolith capability by capability until it can be deleted.

The hardest challenge is always the shared database. In the monolith, tables are joined freely and foreign keys enforce integrity. When I move Payment out, it gets its own database and can no longer join the accounts table, so I replace that join with a call to the Account Service or a local read model kept fresh by events. Integrity that used to be a foreign key becomes an application-level check plus reconciliation, and a transfer that used to be one local transaction becomes a saga with compensating actions, which means accepting eventual consistency.

The other challenges are operational and testing: more pipelines, service discovery, distributed tracing with a shared traceId, and contract tests so a change in one service does not silently break another. The judgment I always emphasize is restraint. I decompose only where teams genuinely need independent deployment or scaling, I extract incrementally, and I am willing to stop or even merge a service back if the boundary turns out to create coordination without autonomy.
